messages.content:
A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across a river.

- If left together **without the farmer**, the wolf eats the goat, and the
  goat eats the cabbage. (Nothing is ever eaten while the farmer is present,
  including in the boat.)
- The boat carries the farmer plus **up to two** of the three items.
- Every crossing of the river — in either direction, loaded or empty —
  counts as one crossing.

Read the constraints carefully; this is not quite the puzzle you may
remember. What is the **minimum total number of crossings** the farmer needs
to get all three items safely to the far side? Show the crossing plan, then
reply with the number.


When you are finished, output your final answer on its own line, as the last line of your response, in the exact format:
ANSWER: <your answer>

text:
**Crossing plan (minimum = 3)** Let **L** be the near side and **R** the far side. The farmer is always in the boat when it moves, so “empty” means he returns alone without any goods. | # | Move (direction) | What’s on board | State after move (left / right) | Why safe? | |---|------------------|-----------------|----------------------------------|-----------| | 1 | **L → R** | Farmer + Wolf + Cabbage | **Left:** Goat alone
**Right:** Farmer, Wolf, Cabbage together (farmer watches them) | No conflict on left; right side has farmer present. | | 2 | **R → L** | Farmer returns **alone** (boat empty of goods) | **Left:** Farmer + Goat together
**Right:** Wolf & Cabbage alone (wolf does not eat cabbage) | Both banks safe: wolf + cabbage don’t interact, and the farmer is present on left. | | 3 | **L → R** | Farmer takes Goat across | **Left:** empty after departure
**Right:** Farmer, Wolf, Goat, Cabbage together (farmer watches all) | All items now safely at far side; no conflict possible with the farmer watching. | All three trips count as one crossing each, so the total is **3**. **Why fewer than 3 crossings cannot work:** - The boat can carry only two of the three items plus the farmer. Hence a single forward trip can never bring all three items across at once; at least one item must stay behind after any first arrival on the far side. - After that, someone (or something) must bring the boat back to fetch the remaining item(s), requiring another crossing. Consequently, with two crossings you could either: * move everything in one go (impossible by capacity), or * leave an unsafe pair alone while returning empty (violates rules). Thus **3** is the minimal possible number of river crossings. ANSWER: 3
